opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a great question, because I think my advisor's perspective changed how I think about research more than almost anything else in my PhD.

Coming from a traditional robotics background, my advisor always cared about one thing first: does it actually work on the robot? Not on a benchmark, not in a simulator with perfect state information, but on real hardware, in the messy real world, with sensor noise, latency, and contact dynamics you can't fully model. Early on, I came in with more of a machine learning mindset, where you propose a method, you show a few percentage points of improvement on some standard dataset, and you write a paper. My advisor would gently push back and ask, "Okay, but what problem does this solve? Why would a roboticist care?"

That question stuck with me. In classical robotics there's a strong culture of understanding *why* something works. You think about structure: kinematics, dynamics, the geometry of the problem, what guarantees you can make. So when I started working on learning-based methods, I was always asked to articulate what assumptions the method makes, and where it would fail. That turned out to be really valuable, because a lot of learning research looks impressive but is brittle in ways that only show up when you deploy it.

The second thing I took away is respect for the baselines. Traditional methods, like a well-tuned controller or a good motion planner, are often very hard to beat. My advisor would say, "If a simple classical approach gets you 90% of the way, your learned method needs to justify its complexity." That forced me to be honest about where learning truly adds value. And I came to believe that learning is most useful where modeling is genuinely hard, like rich contact, deformable objects, or messy perception, not as a replacement for everything we already know how to do well.

So I'd say the biggest lesson was: useful machine learning research in robotics isn't about chasing numbers. It's about combining the right structure with the right amount of learning, and validating it in the real world. Some of the best ideas come from that tension between the robotics view, which wants reliability and understanding, and the ML view, which wants scale and generality. Living in that tension, rather than picking one side, is what I think makes the work meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says the advisor prioritized whether a method works on real hardware and learned that robotics research should be validated in the real world.

r002.rationale: It contrasts an ML mindset focused on benchmark improvements with real-world deployment, but does not communicate that researchers specializing in an emerging field may give insufficient attention to deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
My advisor came from classical robotics, the world of control theory, kinematics, planning under hard physical constraints. So when I showed up excited about deep learning, the first question was never "how good is your benchmark number." It was always "what does this actually do on a robot, and when does it break."

That reframed everything for me. In the traditional view, a method is only useful if you understand its failure modes. A controller with a stability guarantee that performs a bit worse is often more valuable than a black box that performs great until it doesn't. Learning to think that way made me suspicious of results that only lived in simulation or on curated datasets, and it pushed me to ask what assumptions a learned model was quietly making about the world.

It also taught me respect for the problem itself. Roboticists spend years on things like contact, friction, sensor noise, latency. Those aren't details you abstract away; they are the problem. So the ML research I came to find useful wasn't the flashiest architecture. It was work that engaged honestly with those constraints, that gave you something you could deploy, debug, and reason about.

I'd say the lasting lesson is that usefulness is defined by the person who has to trust the system, not by the person publishing the paper. That perspective still guides how I pick problems today.

r001.rationale: The response says the advisor taught Kay to ask what a method does on a robot and describes useful ML research as work that can be deployed, debugged, and reasoned about.

r002.rationale: It criticizes benchmark-focused results and work limited to simulation or curated datasets, but does not clearly say that researchers specializing in an emerging field may neglect deployment.

astra-6.text:
It pushed me to ask what a learning method actually enables a robot to do. From a traditional robotics perspective, better performance on a benchmark is only part of the story. You also care about how the method fits into the system, what assumptions it makes, and what happens when those assumptions break.

That shaped my understanding of usefulness: are we solving a real bottleneck, and does learning make the overall system more capable or more reliable? Sometimes the right answer is a learning method, and sometimes a simpler approach is enough. The important thing is to start with the problem rather than with the technique you want to use.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what a method enables a robot to do and whether it improves the overall system, but it does not say that deployment on real robots is a necessary standard Kay learned from his advisor.

sol-6.1.text: My advisor’s traditional robotics perspective pushed me to ask what a learning method actually enables a robot to do. You can improve a metric on a dataset, but does that translate into better behavior in the real world? Does it solve a problem that was difficult before, and does it work reliably under the constraints of the system? That shaped my understanding of usefulness: the learning algorithm is one part of a larger system, and the research matters when its improvements make a meaningful difference to the task.

r001.rationale: The response says useful research should improve a robot’s real-world behavior, but it does not identify deployment on real robots as a necessary standard.
